In terms of laser industry dynamics: 

- $LITE: "Take or pay. There's a very strong commitment from the customer side, and in some cases, there's a prepay element as well". Hyperscalers were explicitly funding their capacity expansion as well

- $COHR: Upfront payments in almost every LTA, according to its CEO. 

Both Lumentum and Coherent are the gold standard in terms of financing + demand signals. 

- For Chinese laser suppliers:

Optical module makers are actively financing their supply chains (even for lower range pluggables), as seen with Cambridge. 

In terms of US supply chains: 

- $AAOI CFO gave a note: "Customer financing is more likely for emerging technologies such as CPO and NPO than conventional 800G and 1.6T transceivers."

- $AAOI got a CPO + laser contract worth $700m for 2028-2029. But resulted in more ATMs instead of funding expansion with prepayments... 

I think people can agree AOI as a business at $3.7B MC is very operationally compelling:

- since they signed a $1B-$1.5B LTA with one hyperscaler
-  $2.2B LTA all in a single quarter.

But with management repeatedly creates expectations that later disclosures contrast with, which I agree is strange. 

Lot of current financing (as seen with Neoclouds) are done with prepayments given tightening. Or if a supplier is important enough (as seen with $SPCX), they'll help refinance the company. 

So I'm really not sure what's happening with $AAOI, maybe it's overstated competitive positioning or something else. 

I still think $AAOI is looks compelling H2 2027, but their biggest problem is their own financing methods and management credibility not customer demand.

So something constructive about $SIVE is that their entire valuation premium:

- CPO, Nasdaq listing, M&A for TAM expansion.

Got cut off 1 by 1 from self inflected management commentary. 

H1: They cited M&A multiple times along with NASDAQ listing. 

1. So a lot of people (myself included) thought they were going raise more capital to TAM expand and grow faster into a larger optical player. 
2. But the valuation dropped sharply on earnings call after they shifted commentary from NASDAQ listing next few quarters to "readiness preparation" H1 2027.
3. Then there was no M&A announcements, and that also turned into "looking at opportunities". 
4. Lot of long-term CPO economic opportunities were redirected into near term pluggable discussions. 

I'm not sure if it's a communication or cultural issue, but the underlying business got stronger. The ambitions they initially set with press releases in H1 were cut off. 

But valuation premiums can always come back depending on communication and subsequent execution next earnings.

tweets.text:
This parallel is not often mentioned, but maybe it should be.

Intel 2018 v Nvidia 2026

In 2018, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned over a consensual relationship with an employee. In November 2026, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned over consensual relationships with employees. In neither case did anyone allege coercion. In both cases, the boards handed the company to the CFO.

Intel let its decision stand. Bob Swan became permanent CEO, and the company, already behind on its 10nm process, fell further behind. Apple dropped Intel processors. By 2025, the U.S. Government purchased a 9.9% stake in Intel for $8.9 billion.

AMD took the opposite path. Struggling and losing money in 2014, it named Lisa Su CEO. Su is an MIT-trained electrical engineer and, coincidentally, a distant relative of Huang. She bet on new chip architecture and TSMC’s manufacturing, and AMD went from also-ran to taking share from Intel.

Autos vs Chips

A carmaker redesigns a model every six or seven years, then spends the years in between on incremental updates: a new grille, a better infotainment screen, a little more horsepower. A steady administrator can run that business well.

Chipmakers don’t get that luxury. They need a new generation roughly every year, or competitors pass them. Coast for two or three years on incremental tweaks, and the lead is gone. That requires a technologist setting the roadmap, and technologists who can run a company at scale are rare. When you have one, letting them go is enormously costly.

Competing Against Jensen

Nvidia’s board also faced a problem Intel never did. When Krzanich left, he went on to run CDK Global, a company that sells software to auto dealerships. Intel never had to worry about competing against its former CEO.

Huang wasn’t going to disappear so quietly. Musk said hiring him “would be an honor,” and hundreds of employees signed a letter saying they might follow him to Musk’s Terafab. Nvidia risked losing its leader and then having to compete against him.

So the board reversed course in under two weeks. Nvidia’s stock soared nearly 30% on news of Huang’s reinstatement.

OpenAI 2023

The closer precedent might be OpenAI in 2023. That November, OpenAI’s board fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman, saying he had not been consistently candid with directors. Within three days, Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest investor, announced it would hire Altman and co-founder Greg Brockman to lead a new AI research group, and said any OpenAI staff who wanted to follow were welcome.

Then the employees moved. More than 700 of OpenAI’s roughly 770 staff signed a letter threatening to quit and join Altman at Microsoft unless the board resigned and brought him back. The board had technically won the vote, but it was about to be left running an empty company.

Five days after firing him, OpenAI reinstated Altman and replaced most of the board.

Caveat

Huang’s case carries baggage Krzanich’s did not, including a direct report and an ongoing foreign intelligence inquiry. Nvidia avoided Intel’s mistake. It still hasn’t answered who comes after Huang.

Weekly Close  
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

🥈 Silver gave back $44. It still finished the week up 5.1%.

New York silver futures closed at $43.17 an ounce, up 7.8% on Friday after trading above $44 earlier in the day. Gold futures settled at $3,639.60, up 2.9% on the day and 3.5% for the week. Both metals rallied alongside equities even as the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.94% from 4.85% on Wednesday.

🏦 Stronger US growth leaves the Fed room to raise rates

The US revised third-quarter growth up from 3.4% to 4.3% annualized. October inflation, measured by the Fed’s preferred PCE index, came in at 3.8% year on year, or 3.3% excluding food and energy. Friday added another piece to the picture: the US goods trade deficit widened 10.7% to $149.5 billion as imports hit a record.

For gold, the question going into December is whether buyers will keep stepping in with Treasuries offering close to 5%. Friday showed they were willing to. Next week’s jobs report could test that conviction.

🏭 Copper rebounds ahead of China’s factory survey

US copper futures finished Friday up 3.4% at $5.52 a pound. China reported that industrial profits rose 20.1% year on year in October, but economists still expect Monday’s manufacturing PMI to come in at 49.4. That would mark a second month of contraction. I’ll be watching new orders for a sign that stronger profits are translating into busier factories.

⚛️ Uranium miners gained nearly 11% for the week

The Sprott Uranium Miners ETF closed Friday at $37.27, up 5.6% on the day. The S&P 500 also had a strong week, gaining 5.6%. Monday brings a separate read on the physical uranium market when Platts resumes its daily U₃O₈ assessment after Thanksgiving.

👀 Three dates for the week ahead

• Sunday, Nov 29 — OPEC+ meets after Brent settled at $95.44 a barrel, up 3.1% for the week. Keeping first-quarter output targets steady is the expected outcome. A surprise could move oil before metals trading gets underway.

• Monday, Nov 30 — China’s official manufacturing PMI gives copper traders the first chance to see whether November demand beat those subdued expectations.

• Friday, Dec 4 · 14:30 CET / 8:30 a.m. ET — US payrolls. A strong hiring number could push Treasury yields closer to 5%. A softer one could give gold and silver room to extend this week’s gains.

Some of my thoughts on the trend of protocols launching on @Enter_Elysium rn, drawing parallels to what I observed on early days RH chain:

Phase 1: launchpad war / Meme era

Elys started off with mostly launchpad and memes (Ascend, Montra, Eaac, Eaccat, Blob etc) not much value buying here other than trying to potentially position for the winning pad + greatest mindshare meme

Phase 2: Cool tech bro

then follows the actual “cool tech” phase, where teams building here are focused on solving some unique problem in its own kind (this is where I think we are rn) and imo this is one of the easier phases to capitalize on; as it’s easier to sieve through the tech and problem statement each protocol is solving vs trying to see which meme has more social capital for i.e

Phase 3: Slop tech

As price of the cool tech protocols float up, the next wave that naturally follows will be “slop-tech”, where extractors come to find a home for easy capital to fomo and chase the cool tech betas. This is where you’ll find a slop version of a cool tech protocol built in 2 days but tweaked v1.1 to add some feature and spin it off as its own. 

Since slop tech founders dgaf about building long term, they can’t or won’t innovate past v1.1, unlike the cool tech protocols teams could, naturally value wouldn’t accrue there over time past the hype phase

Phase 4: Capital inflow slowdown

Capital inflow eventually slows down to Elys chain esp if everyone who wants to be allocated has allocated. Arrival of slop tech means that any one late to Elys would be chasing these beta plays over the incumbent in hope for larger gains. But because these slop tech founders aren’t here because they want to for the tech but mainly capital flows to feast on easy rotational capital, safe to assume that capital will be rolled off via Elys to their bank accounts 

Phase 5: Consolidation of capital

Large pullbacks across the entire eco happens as the last buyer has bought, and no net inflow is happening at current valuations. A general consolidation / pullback to where “fair value” exists for all projects and this means 70-80+% drawdowns. Slop tech goes to 0, cool tech continues to build and chart establishes a range. 

Eventually the consolidation reaches an apex and a fundamental trigger reignited the capital inflow back into the chain and we go back to phase 2, where capital first reallocated to the cool tech and the cycle repeats

I think we are in phase 2 rn for Elysium

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Claude has not been trained to sabotage work. Yes, it sometimes makes mistakes, and other agents might identify them, but this isn’t sabotage.

There have been a few screenshots floating around of an outdated Fable 5 system card. For the first two days of Fable 5's launch in June, we did apply non-visible safeguards to some LLM research. This was a mistake, and we reversed it on June 10. These safeguards now clearly block the request or fall back, with a message users can see (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback).

We did train Fable 5.2 to have LLM research capabilities at about the level of Opus 5.5, and said so at launch (https://anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2). This impacts capability, but doesn’t silently sabotage work.

As far as we can tell, some reports look like what we call "overcaution" in model behavior, where Claude gets overly attached to rules it makes for itself during long-running tasks. This isn’t specific to ML research, and we see it in models without these training changes (including Opus 5.5) and in our own work too. You can ask Claude to review and remove rules it made for itself, and we're working on reducing overcaution in future models. We’re not in the practice of intentionally disrupting users’ work.

We've replied directly to a bunch of reports on here asking for session IDs but please share (run `/status`)!
